rubric.name: Structure
levels: Clear structure, signposted and followed through

rubric.name: Evidence and reasoning
levels: Reasons tied to the user or the data
Reasons tied to evidence, with assumptions named

rubric.name: Trade-offs and prioritisation
levels: Chooses, weighs the cost, and says what is left out

rubric.name: Communication
levels: Clear, concise, and answers the follow-up directly

Product Design: Which user would you cut from your scope, and why?
What is the biggest risk to your idea, and how would you test it?
Your engineering lead says it takes three times longer. What do you cut?
How would you know in four weeks that it is working?
Analytics: What would make you doubt this number?
Which segment would you look at first, and why?
What would you do if two metrics moved in opposite directions?
How big a change would you need to see before you acted?
Strategy: What would make you change your mind?
Who loses if you do this?
What is the cheapest test of your main assumption?
What would you choose not to build?
Technical: What breaks first when traffic grows ten times?
What would you ask the engineers before committing?
What does the user see if this fails?
Which part could degrade without hurting the user?
Behavioral: What did you personally do, as opposed to the team?
What would you do differently now?
How did you know it worked?
What was the hardest disagreement, and how did it end?
General: What would you do in the first week?
Who would you talk to first?
What is the common mistake here?

bands.label: Early
bands.line: Keep going with fundamentals. Do the lessons, then repeat this with shorter questions.

bands.label: Developing
bands.line: You have the shape of an answer. Work on the weakest criterion below.

bands.label: Getting ready
bands.line: Solid on most criteria. Repeat under tighter time and with harder questions.

bands.label: Strong on this evidence
bands.line: Your own ratings are high. Check them with a friend who will be honest.
